newsitem.title: USA: What difference a legal entity makes.
newsitem.headline: What difference a legal entity makes.

text.p: New entrepreneurs often have a clear idea of where the business should go and are very qualified professionally to make it succeed. But if they're not careful at the outset in choosing a legal entity for their business, they could be setting themselves up for trouble.
The two primary areas affected are taxes and legal liability, both of which are crucial.
The right choice not only could protect you from personal liability should someone sue your business, they also could save you thousands of dollars in taxes.

"There's a whole range of people we come across who usually have a concept in mind, have very little capital and know how to do professionaly what they do. But they don't have any idea of the legal format to take and how to integrate their personal financial positions with their business," said Kevin Sheridan, a partner in Roberts, Sheridan & Kotel, a New York law firm that specialises in advising new business owners.

"I can put in a global area-wide network, but I can't speak knowledgably about why I'm a Limited Liability Corporation," said Jeff Drew, a Sheridan client who started his Netgain LLC telecommunications consulting firm in January.

"Kevin spent a more than reasonable amount of time with me and potential partners explaining partnership. It separated the spectators from the people who were going to do it," he said. "I started out with three partners and ended up with just one and then two people."
Most people may have a general idea of the differences between a mom and pop sole proprietorship and a corporation, but there are numerous other business entities that should be considered.
The number of possible business entities varies by state.

In Missouri, for example, about 15 different legal entities are available. Their titles range from Sole Proprietorship and General or Limited Partnership, to others that only state or federal bureaucrats could come up with, like C or Subchapter S Corporation, Limited Liability Company and even Limited Liability Limited Partnership.

"There has been an absolute explosion in choice of entity," said Jay Nathanson, a principal at the law firm Rosenblum, Goldenhersh, Silverstein & Zafft, P.C. in Clayton, Mo., who also lectures on business entities at the Washington University Law School in St. Louis. "They all have subtle differences, and they all need to be considered with a professional."

As you can see, it's not simple. So before you fork over the $20 fee at your local secretary of state's office to register your business, make an appointment with a qualified attorney to go over the options and decide which is suited to you and your enterprise.

You should expect to pay for initial legal advice and then about $1,000 to form the legal entity. It should not vary much by state, and while many people forgo hiring an attorney for this purpose, chances are it may prevent other spending at a later stage.

"There are tremendous variances from state to state," said Nathanson. "The law in Idaho may be completely different than in New York. In addition, some states have said they won't follow the new federal rules."
Both Nathanson and Sheridan use similar methods to ascertain what legal entity would best serve their clients.
"I have a series of questions that would lead me to give advice on what form it should take," said Sheridan. "The questions are pretty simple and may be obvious, but they do help."

For example, he asks whether the entrepreneur intends to run the venture alone or with partners, be the sole employee or have employees. The answers directly affect how complicated the structure should be and how much flexibility it will require in the future.
Sheridan also asks how the business will be financed.

"Based on the answer, a certain legal form may be preferred," he said. "For example, a Subchapter S corporation is a form historically used by privately held small business. It allows partnership tax treatment of the business -- you can move cash up from the business to the owner without paying a corporate tax in the middle. Similarly, you can allocate the losses of the business to the owner to shelter other income."

Historically, though, there was a problem if you wanted to raise venture capital. A third-party investor might want to receive preferred stock. The old form of Subchapter S did not allow for that, and though the rules have recently been amended, there are still significant restrictions, he said.
"All of this is usually new to the people we are dealing with," said Sheridan.

His firm generally advises people to form a C Corp., or a Limited Liability Company if they intend to seek outside financing. "If they don't and they're just content to run a small business and they aren't going to have any more than a few family or friends as co-owners, very often just a Subchapter 2 status is favourable because they get that favourable tax treatment."
A business can change forms midstream, but it often involves a very expensive process of running of two sets of books for a period of time.
"The message is that the first form that you choose is an important choice, and transforming the form should only be done with a good small-business accountant and possibly a lawyer," said Sheridan.
According to Dun & Bradstreet, a study of more than 4 million businesses formed between 1990 and 1996 showed growth in corporate entities, while proprietorships and partnerships were down.

"Clearly the trend line is toward corporations, with partnerships down more than proprietorships," said Larry Winters, of the company's Small Business Services unit in Parsippany, N.J. "It's very, very consistent growth year after year. I think the kinds of smaller companies we're seeing now are a lot more professional than what we saw earlier."

The number of corporations grew by 5.3 percent over the period, while the other two formations declined by more than 2.5 percent each among businesses with 50 or fewer employees. The study did not break down the corporate sector into the various types of corporate entities.
